seoDescription: Discover the new MCP Tools in Flowise and understand how they differ from traditional LangChain tools. This tutorial guides you through adding and configuring MCP servers for your AI agents, starting with a practical Brave Search integration. Learn about the limitations of using pre-built MCP servers and see a step-by-step demonstration of how to connect a custom MCP server, like a to-do list manager, to your Flowise agent, enhancing its capabilities with new, developer-built functionalities.

summary:
## Understanding MCP Tools vs. Standard Tools

- **Standard Tools** in Flowise are historically based on the **LangChain** library. This creates a dependency where Flowise can only offer tools that have been developed and integrated by LangChain.
- **MCP (Model-Component-Protocol) Tools** represent a new, standardized way to build tools for AI agents. This approach decouples tools from a specific framework like LangChain, allowing any developer or application owner (e.g., Airbnb) to create their own **MCP servers** for integration.
- This new standard should lead to a **larger variety** of available tools for AI agents.

## Integrating an Existing MCP Server: Brave Search

To add a pre-packaged MCP tool like Brave Search to your Flowise agent:

1.  Add a **Tool Agent**, a **Chat Model** (e.g., ChatOpenAI), and a **Memory** node to your canvas.
2.  Go to **MCP Tools** and drag the **Brave Search** node onto the canvas.
3.  Create new **credentials** using your Brave Search API key.
4.  Save the flow and **refresh the page**. The **Available Actions** dropdown will now populate with the server's tools (e.g., `web-search`, `local-search`).
5.  Select the actions you want the agent to use and save the chatflow.

## Integrating a Custom MCP Server

To connect a custom, locally-hosted MCP server to Flowise:

1.  Drag the **Custom MCP Tool** node onto the canvas and connect it to your agent.
2.  In the configuration field, provide a JSON object with two keys: `"Command"` and `"Arguments"`.
3.  Set the `"Command"` to `"node"`.
4.  Set `"Arguments"` to an array containing the path to your server's main JavaScript file (e.g., `"C:\\Users\\...\\index.js"`).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> At the time of recording, Flowise does not support `npx` commands for running MCP servers. You can only run local files using the `node` command.

> [!TIP]
> After configuring the custom tool, save the chatflow and refresh the node's **actions list** to see the tools exposed by your custom server.

## Agent Intelligence with Multiple Tools

The video demonstrates an agent's ability to reason and use multiple tools to accomplish a task. When asked to remove a to-do item by name:

1.  The agent first attempted to call the `remove-todo` tool with the item's text, which **failed** because the tool requires a unique ID.
2.  Recognizing the failure, the agent then automatically called the `get-todos` tool to retrieve the list of all items and their IDs.
3.  Finally, it used the correct ID to successfully call the `remove-todo` tool, completing the user's request.
transcription:
## Introducing MCP Tools in Flowise

Hey there, I hope you're doing well. After updating to the latest version of Flowise, you'll notice this new menu called MCP Tools, just below the usual Tools menu. So what is MCP Tools and how does it differ from the normal Tools menu?

So in this video, we'll try to find that answer, and we'll also have a look at adding a few MCP Tools, including a custom MCP tool to our AI agent.

## LangChain Tools vs. MCP Tools

Now, what's the difference between this normal Tools menu, which includes stuff like Brave Search and the MCP Tools menu, which also seems to include Brave Search as an example? Well, to make sense of this, we have to look at the history of Flowise. Flowise uses a library called LangChain under the hood, and LangChain is a technical framework that developers can use to build AI-driven solutions. And this is used by a lot of other platforms and not just Flowise. It's used by N8N and LangFlow as well.

And historically, Flowise was nothing more than a UI wrapper around this LangChain library. So instead of you having to write code, all you had to do was drag and drop nodes onto a canvas. And if we go to the JavaScript documentation for LangChain, we can go to Integrations, and here you will see all the technical components. So if I click on Chat Models as an example, we can see all the different providers in this list along with the code on how to call this provider, like ChatOpenAI. And we can see the same thing in Flowise, where we can go to Chat Models, and here we can simply add the ChatOpenAI node onto this canvas. So instead of having to write code to access ChatOpenAI, in Flowise, we simply drag and drop a node onto the canvas.

The same goes for tools. So if we go to Tools, we can see all the available tools that were developed by LangChain, and most of these tools were simply exposed within Flowise, the same way they exposed the Chat model. Now this does come with a restriction. Let's say you wanted a tool that could integrate with Airbnb. Now going through the list of tools developed by LangChain, there is no Airbnb tool. Therefore, you will not find that tool in Flowise either.

Now Flowise does give you an option to build your own tools using the Custom tool. In here, you can actually create your own tool, and write a JavaScript code to build out that integration with something like Airbnb. Now if you're not a developer, that might not be ideal, and effectively you are at the mercy of waiting for LangChain to develop that tool for you, or you'll simply have to learn how to build that tool yourself.

## What is MCP?

Now let's talk about MCP tools. MCP is a relatively new concept, and it's really just there to standardize the way developers build tools for AI agents. This is very much a technical concept that's meant for developers, but to explain it simply, application owners like Airbnb can develop their own tools that any agent can consume to interact with their platform. So this means we no longer have that dependency on LangChain, but instead application owners and developers can build their very own MCP servers, as it's called, to create integrations with their own platforms.

So in theory, we should have access to a much larger variety of tools, and it should be easier for developers to build their very own tools. In fact, I've built a very simple to-do MCP server, which we can use to add and list our to-do items, and we will have a look at that in this video. Now first, let's have a look at how we can use these tools, what the potential limitations are, and how we can add a custom MCP server to our AI agent.

## Adding the Brave Search MCP Tool

So let's start by adding an agent, and let's add our tool agent to the canvas. Let's also add our chat model. So on the chat models, let's add chat openAI, and let's add this to our agent. I'll select my credentials, and for the model, I'll actually just leave it on GPT for O-mini. We also need to add a memory node. So on the memory, let's add buffer memory, and let's add it to our agent. Cool.

Now, let's have a look at adding an MCP tool. So let's scroll down to MCP tools, and here we have access to a few tools, like Brave Search, a custom MCP tool, GitHub, PostgreSQL, and Slack. So at the moment, there aren't many tools listed, and I will imagine that Flowise we'll be adding a lot of different tools in the near future. For now, let's use the Brave Search tool, like so, and let's attach it to our agent. Now, under the credentials, let's create a new credential, and now we have to provide our Brave Search API key. I'll just call this credential, Brave Search YouTube demo, and for the API key, let's go to brave.com, and let's sign up for an account. The service is free to use, and you will not be charged a thing. So just go to the setup process, and then go to API keys, then create a new API key. I'll just call mine Flow-wise demo, then copy your key, and add it to Flow-wise. Right, now under the list of actions, we don't see any actions yet, and if we click on refresh, and click on this dropdown, you might not see anything either. So if we save this flow, refresh this page, then under available actions, we can now see all the different tools that are exposed by this Brave Search MCP server.

## Testing the Brave Search Integration

We've got local search, which is ideal for finding local businesses, and we also have web search. Let's click on this tool. Of course, we are able to assign more than one tool as well. So we could also just add local search. I'll just use web search for now. It states this by saving the chat flow, and it's Oscar agent something like, what is the new OpenAI responses API about, and how does it affect the assistance API? And let's send this.

And right, looking at this response, this does seem correct. First, we can see that Brave Search was indeed called, so the tool definitely works. And we can see the API is faster and more flexible, and cool. So, and this is how we can add an existing MCP server to Flow-wise.

## Limitations & Custom MCP Server Overview

Now, I do want to mention one limitation before we move on to adding our own custom MCP server. Some of you might be wondering if you are able to add any of these existing servers yourself. So if you go to GitHub and servers, we can scroll down and find a whole list of example servers. So at the moment, we have Brave Search embedded into Flow-wise, but as you can see, there are plenty of other servers as well, including the file system server, which allows your agent to write and read files on your operating system.

Now, usually what you would do if you are using something like cursor or claw desktop, is you would simply add this by scrolling down, and you would add the server using this NPX command. Unfortunately, the NPX commands do not work in Flow-wise at the time of recording. If this does change, I will create a follow-up video. You can build your own MCP servers and attach it to Flow-wise as well.

I built my own custom MCP server, which allows me to store and retrieve to-do items. Now, I've created a separate video on building that MCP server, and I will link to it in the description of this video, and the card should show up on your screen right now. Now, this is a coding tutorial, which I'm not going to go into detail in this video, so if you are interested in learning how to build this, or if you just want to copy my solution across and use it immediately, then check out that video.

## Configuring a Custom MCP Tool in Flowise

But the server offers a few tools. There's a tool to add new to-do items, it's a separate tool for getting the to-dos, and we also have a tool for removing to-do items.

Now, all we have to do is copy the path to the index file, so I'll simply copy this path, then let's go to Add Nodes, and on the tools MCP, let's add the custom MCP tool, and let's go ahead and attach it to our tool agent in the meantime. Then, to add a custom tool, we need to provide the following. Let's provide an object with opening and closing curly braces, then we need to provide two properties. The first is Command, and the second is Arguments, and this is an array of values.

Now, for the command, as I mentioned earlier, we cannot use npx, and we can only use node. This simply means we can run a file that exists on our local machine, like this index file that I just copied from my code editor. Now, in the arguments, we need to specify the path to that index file, so I'll just paste this in, and I'll just add another backslash to each of these backslashes just to escape it. So, I'll just do this, and lastly, let's save this. Let's save this chat flow. If we refresh the actions, we can see all the tools pulling in from our MCP server. How cool is that? So, let's add add to do, let's also add get to do, and let's add remove to do. Let's save this flow, and let's test this out.

## Demonstrating the Custom To-Do Agent

So, I'll just start a new chat, and let's start by asking, please list my to do items, and we can see it's called a tool, and the tool returned one item. Let's add an item by saying, please add a to do item called call mom. And it's saying I've added the to do item called mom. Looking at the stool call, we can see that add to do was indeed called with the text call mom. So, if you ask again, list my to dos. It now says we've got two items, call mom and subscribe to Leon, and we can see it in the response of the tool calls as well.

Lastly, let's say, please remove the item called call mom. And what's cool about this is initially, it tried to call the remove to do, which failed because the remove to do tool expects the unique ID and not the text. So, the agent then figured out that it had to call the tool to get that ID, and then it successfully called the remove to do item.

## Conclusion

So, what are your thoughts on MCP tools? Is this something you'll use in your workflows? Are you planning to build your very own MCP servers, or will you just stick to the old way of doing things? If you like this video, hit the like button, subscribe to my channel, and I'll see you in the next one.
